The combination of these heuristic neurons (a bag of heuristics) explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts.
This mechanism emerges early in training and persists as the main source of arithmetic accuracy.
The bag of heuristics fails to generalize perfectly, leading to errors when prompts lack sufficient associated heuristics or when heuristics have imperfect recall.
papers.limitation:
Human bias in defining heuristic types, as abstractions are based on human-identifiable definitions.
Analysis focuses on LLMs that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens, which may not generalize to models with single-digit tokenization.
future_direction: Developing methods to identify heuristic abstractions without human bias.
Investigating if regularization can improve the bag of heuristics mechanism.
Exploring fundamental changes to training and architectures to improve mathematical abilities.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) solve reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms, or do they memorize training data? To investigate this question, we use arithmetic reasoning as a representative task. Using causal analysis, we identify a subset of the model (a circuit) that explains most of the model's behavior for basic arithmetic logic and examine its functionality. By zooming in on the level of individual circuit neurons, we discover a sparse set of important neurons that implement simple heuristics. Each heuristic identifies a numerical input pattern and outputs corresponding answers. We hypothesize that the combination of these heuristic neurons is the mechanism used to produce correct arithmetic answers. To test this, we categorize each neuron into several heuristic types-such as neurons that activate when an operand falls within a certain range-and find that the unordered combination of these heuristic types is the mechanism that explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts. Finally, we demonstrate that this mechanism appears as the main source of arithmetic accuracy early in training. Overall, our experimental results across several LLMs show that LLMs perform arithmetic using neither robust algorithms nor memorization; rather, they rely on a "bag of heuristics".

papers.title: Towards a Mechanistic Understanding of Propositional Logical Reasoning in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How do large language models internally perform propositional logical reasoning? What computational strategies do they employ?
papers.core_contribution: The paper identifies a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning in Qwen3 models, comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation, Information Transmission, Fact Retrospection, and Specialized Attention Heads.
papers.conclusion: The investigation uncovers a coherent computational architecture for propositional logical reasoning, with four interlocking mechanisms that generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, suggesting fundamental computational strategies rather than task-specific shortcuts.
papers.key_findings:
The model organizes reasoning into staged computation: early layers process facts, middle layers process logical expressions, and late layers aggregate for prediction.
Information transmission occurs through segment-terminal tokens (boundary tokens) that act as information hubs.
Fact retrospection: the model persistently re-accesses source fact tokens throughout the network depth.
Specialized attention heads: splitting heads (early layers), transmission heads (middle layers), and fact-retrieval heads (middle to late layers) implement the above mechanisms.
These mechanisms generalize across model scales (8B and 14B), rule types (11 categories), and reasoning depths (one-hop and two-hop).
papers.limitation:
The internal computations within MLP layers remain largely unexplored.
The analysis does not explain how or when these mechanisms emerge during training.
Cannot definitively rule out that these patterns reflect sophisticated statistical shortcuts rather than genuine logical algorithms.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to deeper reasoning chains (i.e., three-hop and beyond).
Investigating diverse model architectures beyond the Qwen family (e.g., Llama, Mistral, etc.).
Analyzing training dynamics to reveal how and when these mechanisms emerge during pretraining.
papers.abstract: Understanding how Large Language Models (LLMs) perform logical reasoning internally remains a fundamental challenge. While prior mechanistic studies focus on identifying taskspecific circuits, they leave open the question of what computational strategies LLMs employ for propositional reasoning. We address this gap through comprehensive analysis of Qwen3 (8B and 14B) on PropLogic-MI, a controlled dataset spanning 11 propositional logic rule categories across one-hop and two-hop reasoning. Rather than asking ''which components are necessary,'' we ask ''how does the model organize computation?'' Our analysis reveals a coherent computational architecture comprising four interlocking mechanisms: Staged Computation (layer-wise processing phases), Information Transmission (information flow aggregation at boundary tokens), Fact Retrospection (persistent re-access of source facts), and Specialized Attention Heads (functionally distinct head types). These mechanisms generalize across model scales, rule types, and reasoning depths, providing mechanistic evidence that LLMs employ structured computational strategies for logical reasoning.

papers.title: How Do LLMs Use Their Depth?
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally structure their computations during inference and use their depth layer-by-layer to arrive at predictions?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a 'Guess-then-Refine' framework showing that LLMs use early layers for statistical guesses (high-frequency tokens) and later layers for contextual refinement, with depth usage varying by task complexity.
papers.conclusion: LLMs are early statistical guessers and late contextual integrators, using depth flexibly based on task complexity.
papers.key_findings:
Early LLM layers propose high-frequency tokens as statistical guesses due to lack of contextual information.
Early layer guesses are heavily refined in later layers, with 80% of early top-ranked guesses replaced.
In multiple-choice tasks, early layers collect valid options and later layers reason between them.
In multi-token fact recall, the first token requires more computational depth than subsequent tokens.
Function words (e.g., determiners, prepositions) are predicted correctly earlier than content words (nouns, verbs).
papers.limitation: Analysis limited to next-token prediction, fact recall, and downstream tasks; does not cover reasoning or chain-of-thought tasks.
future_direction: Analysis for reasoning and chain-of-thought tasks
Analysis of more recent reasoning models
papers.abstract: Growing evidence suggests that large language models do not use their depth uniformly, yet we still lack a fine-grained understanding of their layer-wise prediction dynamics. In this paper, we trace the intermediate representations of several open-weight models during inference and reveal a structured and nuanced use of depth. Specifically, we propose a "Guess-then-Refine" framework that explains how LLMs internally structure their computations to make predictions. We first show that the top-ranked predictions in early LLM layers are composed primarily of high-frequency tokens, which act as statistical guesses proposed by the model early on due to the lack of appropriate contextual information. As contextual information develops deeper into the model, these initial guesses get refined into contextually appropriate tokens. Even high-frequency token predictions from early layers get refined >70% of the time, indicating that correct token prediction is not "one-and-done". We then go beyond frequency-based prediction to examine the dynamic usage of layer depth across three case studies. (i) Part-of-speech analysis shows that function words are, on average, the earliest to be predicted correctly. (ii) Fact recall task analysis shows that, in a multi-token answer, the first token requires more computational depth than the rest. (iii) Multiple-choice task analysis shows that the model identifies the format of the response within the first half of the layers, but finalizes its response only toward the end. Together, our results provide a detailed view of depth usage in LLMs, shedding light on the layer-by-layer computations that underlie successful predictions and providing insights for future works to improve computational efficiency in transformer-based models.

papers.title: Emergent Specialization: Rare Token Neurons in Language Models
papers.research_question: Do large language models develop internal mechanisms specialized for processing rare tokens during pre-training, and what are the mechanisms for their emergence and behavior?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies rare token neurons in language models and shows they emerge through a three-phase structure during training, with coordinated activation and heavy-tailed weight distributions, suggesting a statistical mechanical basis for emergent specialization.
papers.conclusion: Language models spontaneously develop functionally specialized subnetworks for rare token processing, characterized by a three-phase structure and heavy-tailed weight distributions, suggesting emergent specialization analogous to biological complementary learning systems.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs develop dedicated 'rare token neurons' that disproportionately impact the prediction of infrequent tokens.
These specialized neurons emerge through distinct phase transitions during training, evolving from a homogeneous initial state to a functionally differentiated architecture.
The emergence of specialized neuron groups correlates with the development of heavy-tailed weight distributions.
Rare token neurons form a coordinated subnetwork that selectively co-activates while avoiding co-activation with other neurons.
Neuron influence exhibits a three-phase structure: an influential plateau, a power-law decay phase, and a rapid decay phase.
papers.limitation:
Focus on final MLP layer only, while rare token processing likely involves distributed mechanisms across multiple architectural components.
Reliance on ablation-based proxies to quantify neuron contributions, which lack the theoretical rigor of more principled attribution methods.
Constrained to next-token prediction in autoregressive language modeling, so generalizability to downstream applications is unclear.
future_direction: Examining attention heads, intermediate layers, and cross-layer interactions to provide a more comprehensive understanding of rare token processing mechanisms.
Developing precise theoretical frameworks for measuring neuron-level effects to strengthen mechanistic interpretations.
Investigating rare token processing mechanisms in downstream applications such as question-answering and mathematical reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models struggle with representing and generating rare tokens despite their importance in specialized domains. In this study, we identify neuron structures with exceptionally strong influence on language model's prediction of rare tokens, termed as rare token neurons, and investigate the mechanism for their emergence and behavior. These neurons exhibit a characteristic three-phase organization (plateau, power-law, and rapid decay) that emerges dynamically during training, evolving from a homogeneous initial state to a functionally differentiated architecture. In the activation space, rare token neurons form a coordinated subnetwork that selectively co-activates while avoiding co-activation with other neurons. This functional specialization potentially correlates with the development of heavy-tailed weight distributions, suggesting a statistical mechanical basis for emergent specialization.

papers.title: Word-order Biases in Deep-agent Emergent Communication
papers.research_question: Do sequence-processing neural networks exhibit natural language word-order biases, such as temporal iconicity, avoidance of redundancy, and minimization of long-distance dependencies?
papers.core_contribution: LSTM-based Seq2Seq agents show some natural language word-order biases (like avoiding long-distance dependencies) but not others (like avoiding redundant coding), suggesting the need to incorporate 'effort' to make AI communication more human-like.
papers.conclusion: Seq2Seq agents partially exhibit natural word-order biases, but differ in some aspects (like preference for backward order and weak redundancy avoidance), suggesting incorporating effort-based pressures to make AI communication more human-like.
papers.key_findings:
LSTM agents show a strong tendency to avoid long-distance dependencies.
LSTM agents have a preference for backward-iconic order over forward-iconic, which is opposite to human language.
Only weak tendency towards avoidance of redundant coding (e.g., markers in fixed-order languages).
In iterated learning, free-order languages tend to become more fixed with preferred orders emerging.
Attention-enhanced models learn faster and show some biases more clearly.
future_direction: How to incorporate 'effort'-based pressures in neural networks.
papers.abstract: Sequence-processing neural networks led to remarkable progress on many NLP tasks. As a consequence, there has been increasing interest in understanding to what extent they process language as humans do. We aim here to uncover which biases such models display with respect to "natural" word-order constraints. We train models to communicate about paths in a simple gridworld, using miniature languages that reflect or violate various natural language trends, such as the tendency to avoid redundancy or to minimize long-distance dependencies. We study how the controlled characteristics of our miniature languages affect individual learning and their stability across multiple network generations. The results draw a mixed picture. On the one hand, neural networks show a strong tendency to avoid long-distance dependencies. On the other hand, there is no clear preference for the efficient, non-redundant encoding of information that is widely attested in natural language. We thus suggest inoculating a notion of "effort" into neural networks, as a possible way to make their linguistic behavior more humanlike.

papers.title: Enhancing Multimodal Large Language Models Complex Reason via Similarity Computation
papers.research_question: How can the complex reasoning ability of Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs) be improved by efficiently utilizing image information and filtering out irrelevant image tokens?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds that image tokens semantically related to text have information flow convergence and higher attention scores in the LLM decoder, and proposes Simignore, a method to filter irrelevant image tokens based on similarity computation, which improves complex reasoning performance.
papers.conclusion: The proposed Simignore method, which computes similarity between image and text embeddings to filter irrelevant tokens, enhances the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs.
papers.key_findings:
Image tokens semantically related to text prompts are more likely to have information flow convergence and receive higher attention scores in the LLM decoder.
Filtering out irrelevant image tokens based on similarity between image and text embeddings improves the accuracy of LVLMs on complex reasoning tasks.
The performance improvement depends on the number of tokens ignored, with an optimal number (e.g., 124 out of 576 for LLaVA1.5-7B) yielding the best results.
Important image tokens (with high similarity to text) are crucial for complex reasoning, while unimportant tokens can be ignored to improve performance and reduce computation.
Cosine similarity performs better than Euclidean and Manhattan distance for computing the similarity between image and text embeddings in this task.
papers.limitation:
The method does not adaptively choose the number of image tokens to ignore.
The internal mechanisms of how image and textual information work together to facilitate complex reasoning are not fully understood.
future_direction: Exploring strategies for adaptively choosing the number of image tokens to ignore.
Investigating the internal mechanisms of the model to more fully understand how image and textual information work together.
papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models have experienced rapid growth, and numerous different models have emerged. The interpretability of LVLMs remains an under-explored area. Especially when faced with more complex tasks such as chain-of-thought reasoning, its internal mechanisms still resemble a black box that is difficult to decipher. By studying the interaction and information flow between images and text, we noticed that in models such as LLaVA1.5, image tokens that are semantically related to text are more likely to have information flow convergence in the LLM decoding layer, and these image tokens receive higher attention scores. However, those image tokens that are less relevant to the text do not have information flow convergence, and they only get very small attention scores. To efficiently utilize the image information, we propose a new image token reduction method, Simignore, which aims to improve the complex reasoning ability of LVLMs by computing the similarity between image and text embeddings and ignoring image tokens that are irrelevant and unimportant to the text. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our method for complex reasoning tasks.

papers.title: Unveiling Reasoning Thresholds in Language Models: Scaling, Fine-Tuning, and Interpretability through Attention Maps
papers.research_question: What is the critical parameter threshold for reasoning abilities in decoder-only transformer-based language models, and how can fine-tuning and attention map analysis improve understanding of these capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies a critical parameter threshold (~1.6B) for reasoning abilities in language models, shows fine-tuning improves sub-threshold models, and uses attention maps to interpret reasoning processes.
papers.conclusion: The study identifies a critical parameter threshold for reasoning, demonstrates fine-tuning efficacy for sub-threshold models, and uses attention maps for interpretability, advancing understanding of reasoning in decoder-only transformer-based language models.
papers.key_findings:
Models above ~1.6 billion parameters show significant improvement in reasoning performance on tasks like commonsense QA and deductive reasoning.
Fine-tuning sub-threshold models with task-specific exemplars substantially improves performance on simpler deductive rules (e.g., implication elimination, conjunction introduction).
Attention map analysis reveals that models generating correct chain-of-thought exhibit higher token-level attention scores on subsequent correct tokens and correct parts of speech.
Parameter gaps exist for specific deductive rules: disjunction elimination (~1.1B) and proof by contradiction (~1.6B).
Smaller models (below threshold) struggle with structured answer formatting, resulting in high rates of unparseable responses.
papers.abstract: This study investigates the in-context learning capabilities of various decoder-only transformer-based language models with different model sizes and training data, including GPT2, SmolLM2, OpenELM, TinyLlama, Stable LM, and Gemma 2. We identify a critical parameter threshold (~1.6 billion), beyond which reasoning performance improves significantly in tasks such as commonsense reasoning in multiple-choice question answering and deductive reasoning. Specifically, models above this threshold achieve better success rates in chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting for deductive reasoning tasks, especially those requiring longer reasoning chains, such as proof by contradiction and disjunction elimination. To address limitations in sub-threshold models, we demonstrate that fine-tuning with task-specific exemplars substantially enhances reasoning performance, enabling accurate CoT generation even without additional exemplars in the prompt for tasks with shorter reasoning chains. Finally, our analysis of attention maps reveals that models capable of generating correct CoTs exhibit higher token-level attention scores on subsequent correct tokens and the correct parts of speech, providing interpretability insights into reasoning processes. These findings collectively advance understanding of reasoning capabilities in decoder-only transformer-based models. The code is available at: https://github.com/AnnonymousForPapers/CoT_Reasoning_Test.

papers.title: Rethinking embedding coupling in pre-trained language models
papers.research_question: What is the impact of decoupling input and output embeddings in pre-trained language models, and can flexible sizing of these embeddings lead to more efficient parameter allocation and improved performance?
papers.core_contribution: Decoupling input and output embeddings provides modeling flexibility, allowing reduction of input embedding size to save parameters and increase of output embedding size to improve transfer performance, leading to more efficient and effective pre-trained models.
papers.conclusion: Decoupling input and output embeddings and resizing them independently leads to more efficient parameter allocation, improved downstream performance, and more transferable representations, particularly in the upper layers of the Transformer.
papers.key_findings:
Decoupling embedding shapes (not just parameters) provides significant modeling flexibility without consistent performance loss when dimensions remain fixed.
Reducing input embedding dimension saves parameters with minimal performance cost, while increasing output embedding size improves downstream task performance even though the output embedding is discarded after pre-training.
Reinvesting parameters saved from smaller input embeddings into increasing Transformer layer width or depth improves performance on multilingual understanding tasks.
Larger output embeddings prevent the last Transformer layers from over-specializing to the pre-training task, making their representations more transferable across tasks and languages.
The proposed Rebalanced mBERT (RemBERT) model outperforms the state-of-the-art XLM-R on the XTREME benchmark while using 3.5x fewer pre-training tokens.
future_direction: Exploration of alternative strategies for expanding pre-training capacity beyond increasing output embedding size.
papers.abstract: We re-evaluate the standard practice of sharing weights between input and output embeddings in state-of-the-art pre-trained language models. We show that decoupled embeddings provide increased modeling flexibility, allowing us to significantly improve the efficiency of parameter allocation in the input embedding of multilingual models. By reallocating the input embedding parameters in the Transformer layers, we achieve dramatically better performance on standard natural language understanding tasks with the same number of parameters during fine-tuning. We also show that allocating additional capacity to the output embedding provides benefits to the model that persist through the fine-tuning stage even though the output embedding is discarded after pre-training. Our analysis shows that larger output embeddings prevent the model's last layers from overspecializing to the pre-training task and encourage Transformer representations to be more general and more transferable to other tasks and languages. Harnessing these findings, we are able to train models that achieve strong performance on the XTREME benchmark without increasing the number of parameters at the fine-tuning stage.

papers.title: Disentangling Memory and Reasoning Ability in Large Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we disentangle memory recall and reasoning steps in large language models to improve performance and interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: This paper introduces a novel LLM inference paradigm that disentangles memory recall and reasoning steps using special tokens, enhancing both accuracy and interpretability in complex QA tasks.
papers.conclusion: The proposed decomposition of memory and reasoning steps in LLMs leads to improved performance and greater interpretability, enabling better error analysis and model refinement.
papers.key_findings:
The method improves LLM performance on StrategyQA, CommonsenseQA, and TruthfulQA benchmarks, outperforming baselines like CoT and planning tokens.
On TruthfulQA, the enhanced LLaMA-3.1-8B model achieves 86.6% accuracy, surpassing GPT-4o with CoT prompting.
Error analysis reveals that most errors originate from reasoning steps rather than memory recall, highlighting reasoning as the primary challenge.
The decomposition enhances interpretability by allowing clear separation of memory and reasoning steps in the inference process.
Attention analysis shows that special tokens receive higher attention weights, indicating their role in guiding knowledge and reasoning content generation.
papers.limitation:
Dependency on training data quality for memory recall
Token utilization complexity due to special tokens
Performance may struggle with highly complex reasoning tasks
Computation overhead from decomposing steps
future_direction: Dynamic memory updating to incorporate new information without retraining.
Adaptive reasoning steps based on task complexity.
Interpretable error analysis tools for tracing failures to memory or reasoning steps.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance in handling complex tasks requiring both extensive knowledge and reasoning abilities. However, the existing LLM inference pipeline operates as an opaque process without explicit separation between knowledge retrieval and reasoning steps, making the model's decision-making process unclear and disorganized. This ambiguity can lead to issues such as hallucinations and knowledge forgetting, which significantly impact the reliability of LLMs in high-stakes domains. In this paper, we propose a new inference paradigm that decomposes the complex inference process into two distinct and clear actions: (1) memory recall: which retrieves relevant knowledge, and (2) reasoning: which performs logical steps based on the recalled knowledge. To facilitate this decomposition, we introduce two special tokens memory and reason, guiding the model to distinguish between steps that require knowledge retrieval and those that involve reasoning. Our experiment results show that this decomposition not only improves model performance but also enhances the interpretability of the inference process, enabling users to identify sources of error and refine model responses effectively. The code is available at https://github.com/MingyuJ666/Disentangling-Memory-and-Reasoning.

papers.title: A Sentence is Worth a Thousand Pictures: Can Large Language Models Understand Hum4n L4ngu4ge and the W0rld behind W0rds?
papers.research_question: Are humans and LLMs equally accurate in decoding leetspeak, and can they equally explain the substitutions?
papers.core_contribution: Humans outperform LLMs in decoding leetspeak, demonstrating that LLMs lack top-down processing and grounded cognition, which are essential for human-like language understanding.
papers.conclusion: LLMs do not possess human-like linguistic competence; superficial similarity in output does not imply system equivalence, and models lack grounded cognition and top-down processing.
papers.key_findings:
Humans achieve near-ceiling accuracy in decoding leetspeak, while LLMs perform worse.
ChatGPT-4o is the best-performing model but still below humans, especially with more substitutions.
LLMs show an accuracy-reasoning mismatch, often decoding correctly but failing to explain substitutions.
Model errors are qualitatively different from human errors, indicating a lack of common sense and real-world grounding.
Performance differences suggest LLMs rely on form-based associations rather than meaning.
future_direction: Future language models may need to take an entirely different approach, beginning with deeper semantics and cognitive models of the world.
A closer examination of how LLM outputs align with subtle syntactic, acceptability judgments in humans.
Combining deep learning with models of symbolic cognition.
papers.abstract: Modern Artificial Intelligence applications show great potential for language-related tasks that rely on next-word prediction. The current generation of Large Language Models (LLMs) have been linked to claims about human-like linguistic performance and their applications are hailed both as a step towards artificial general intelligence and as a major advance in understanding the cognitive, and even neural basis of human language. To assess these claims, first we analyze the contribution of LLMs as theoretically informative representations of a target cognitive system vs. atheoretical mechanistic tools. Second, we evaluate the models' ability to see the bigger picture, through top-down feedback from higher levels of processing, which requires grounding in previous expectations and past world experience. We hypothesize that since models lack grounded cognition, they cannot take advantage of these features and instead solely rely on fixed associations between represented words and word vectors. To assess this, we designed and ran a novel 'leet task' (l33t t4sk), which requires decoding sentences in which letters are systematically replaced by numbers. The results suggest that humans excel in this task whereas models struggle, confirming our hypothesis. We interpret the results by identifying the key abilities that are still missing from the current state of development of these models, which require solutions that go beyond increased system scaling.

papers.title: In-context Learning and Induction Heads
papers.research_question: Do induction heads constitute the mechanism for the majority of in-context learning in transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: Presents evidence that induction heads, a type of attention head circuit, are the primary mechanism for in-context learning in transformer models.
papers.conclusion: Induction heads likely explain a large fraction of in-context learning in transformers, with strong evidence in small models and correlational evidence in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Induction heads form abruptly during a phase change in training, coinciding with a sharp increase in in-context learning ability.
Altering the transformer architecture to shift the formation of induction heads also shifts the improvement in in-context learning.
Ablating induction heads in small models greatly reduces in-context learning.
Induction heads exhibit general in-context learning behaviors beyond literal copying, such as translation.
The mechanism of induction heads in small models suggests how they could be repurposed for general in-context learning.
papers.limitation: Evidence for large models is correlational and could be confounded by other factors.
future_direction: Establish the claim more firmly with additional evidence
Study the phase change in more detail
papers.abstract: "Induction heads" are attention heads that implement a simple algorithm to complete token sequences like [A][B] ... [A] -> [B]. In this work, we present preliminary and indirect evidence for a hypothesis that induction heads might constitute the mechanism for the majority of all "in-context learning" in large transformer models (i.e. decreasing loss at increasing token indices). We find that induction heads develop at precisely the same point as a sudden sharp increase in in-context learning ability, visible as a bump in the training loss. We present six complementary lines of evidence, arguing that induction heads may be the mechanistic source of general in-context learning in transformer models of any size. For small attention-only models, we present strong, causal evidence; for larger models with MLPs, we present correlational evidence.

papers.title: Extending Token Computation for LLM Reasoning
papers.research_question: What is the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance? Can extending the Chain-of-Thought chain within the same prompt improve reasoning outcomes?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a novel algorithm that extends computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought process by optimizing attention mechanisms, which improves reasoning capabilities, especially in non-STEM domains.
papers.conclusion: The study introduces an attention optimization method that enhances LLM reasoning, particularly in non-STEM domains, and sets the groundwork for more transparent and adaptable models for real-world applications.
papers.key_findings:
Increasing the number of computed tokens enhances LLM reasoning performance.
Attention patterns in middle layers are skewed by non-semantic tokens with high attention scores, which hinders reasoning.
The proposed algorithm re-balances attention distributions by emulating early layer attention patterns, leading to more extended and logical reasoning steps.
The method improves reasoning in non-STEM domains but may reduce accuracy in memory-dependent questions due to error propagation.
Larger models (e.g., 13B) show greater improvement with the method compared to smaller models (e.g., 7B).
papers.limitation:
The method reduces accuracy by 3 percentage points in memory-dependent questions from the MMLU dataset.
Extended reasoning may amplify error propagation in STEM categories where the model's reasoning capabilities are not robust.
Scarcity of logical process examples for STEM questions in training data may hinder performance.
future_direction: Integrate a training phase to enhance memory recall for early-answering questions.
Reduce memory and computational demands using techniques like ghost attention mechanisms.
Enhance interpretability of attention patterns across layers.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are pivotal in advancing natural language processing but often struggle with complex reasoning tasks due to inefficient attention distributions. In this paper, we explore the effect of increased computed tokens on LLM performance and introduce a novel method for extending computed tokens in the Chain-of-Thought (CoT) process, utilizing attention mechanism optimization. By fine-tuning an LLM on a domain-specific, highly structured dataset, we analyze attention patterns across layers, identifying inefficiencies caused by non-semantic tokens with outlier high attention scores. To address this, we propose an algorithm that emulates early layer attention patterns across downstream layers to re-balance skewed attention distributions and enhance knowledge abstraction. Our findings demonstrate that our approach not only facilitates a deeper understanding of the internal dynamics of LLMs but also significantly improves their reasoning capabilities, particularly in non-STEM domains. Our study lays the groundwork for further innovations in LLM design, aiming to create more powerful, versatile, and responsible models capable of tackling a broad range of real-world applications.

papers.title: The Clock and the Pizza: Two Stories in Mechanistic Explanation of Neural Networks
papers.research_question: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably re-discover known algorithms for solving those tasks, and under what conditions do they discover familiar algorithmic solutions?
papers.core_contribution: Neural networks trained on modular addition can discover qualitatively different algorithms (Clock, Pizza, and others), with the algorithm learned depending on hyperparameters like attention rate and width, revealing algorithmic phase transitions and the need for tools to characterize algorithmic phase spaces.
papers.conclusion: Algorithmic discoveries in neural networks are not inevitable; even simple tasks admit a diversity of solutions, motivating the development of tools to characterize the algorithmic phase space of neural networks.
papers.key_findings:
Networks can learn either the previously described Clock algorithm or a new, less intuitive Pizza algorithm for modular addition.
The Pizza algorithm uses averaging and absolute value operations, while the Clock algorithm uses multiplication via attention.
Models sometimes implement multiple, parallel copies of an algorithm (ensembling) for robustness.
Sharp algorithmic phase transitions between Clock and Pizza occur as model hyperparameters (attention rate, width) are varied.
Non-circular algorithms also exist, especially in deeper networks or with low attention rates.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on a single learning problem (modular addition), and scaling the techniques to more complex models and real-world tasks requires significant additional work.
future_direction: How to find, classify, and interpret unfamiliar algorithms in a systematic way.
How to disentangle multiple, parallel algorithm implementations in the presence of ensembling.
papers.abstract: Do neural networks, trained on well-understood algorithmic tasks, reliably rediscover known algorithms for solving those tasks? Several recent studies, on tasks ranging from group arithmetic to in-context linear regression, have suggested that the answer is yes. Using modular addition as a prototypical problem, we show that algorithm discovery in neural networks is sometimes more complex. Small changes to model hyperparameters and initializations can induce the discovery of qualitatively different algorithms from a fixed training set, and even parallel implementations of multiple such algorithms. Some networks trained to perform modular addition implement a familiar Clock algorithm; others implement a previously undescribed, less intuitive, but comprehensible procedure which we term the Pizza algorithm, or a variety of even more complex procedures. Our results show that even simple learning problems can admit a surprising diversity of solutions, motivating the development of new tools for characterizing the behavior of neural networks across their algorithmic phase space.

papers.title: Rethinking the Role of Scale for In-Context Learning: An Interpretability-based Case Study at 66 Billion Scale
papers.research_question: Are all LLM components really needed to perform in-context learning?
papers.core_contribution: The study finds that a large fraction of attention heads (~70%) and feed-forward networks (~20%) in a 66B parameter language model can be removed with minimal decline in in-context learning performance, and that induction heads (capable of primitive operations) overlap with task-important heads.
papers.conclusion: Large language models may be undertrained for in-context learning, opening up questions on how to pre-train them to more effectively perform in-context learning.
papers.key_findings:
Approximately 70% of attention heads can be removed with minimal decline in task performance across 14 NLP tasks.
Approximately 20% of feed-forward networks can be removed with minimal decline in task performance.
Important attention heads are primarily clustered in intermediate layers, while important FFNs are in later layers.
There is substantial overlap in the set of attention heads important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples.
Induction heads (heads scoring highly on prefix matching and copying) overlap with task-specific important heads, suggesting they are capable of more sophisticated in-context learning behaviors.
future_direction: Investigating how to pre-train language models to more effectively perform in-context learning.
papers.abstract: Language models have been shown to perform better with an increase in scale on a wide variety of tasks via the in-context learning paradigm. In this paper, we investigate the hypothesis that the ability of a large language model to in-context learn-perform a task is not uniformly spread across all of its underlying components. Using a 66 billion parameter language model (OPT-66B) across a diverse set of 14 downstream tasks, we find this is indeed the case: $\sim$70% of attention heads and $\sim$20% of feed forward networks can be removed with minimal decline in task performance. We find substantial overlap in the set of attention heads (un)important for in-context learning across tasks and number of in-context examples. We also address our hypothesis through a task-agnostic lens, finding that a small set of attention heads in OPT-66B score highly on their ability to perform primitive induction operations associated with in-context learning, namely, prefix matching and copying. These induction heads overlap with task-specific important heads, reinforcing arguments by Olsson et al. (arXiv:2209.11895) regarding induction head generality to more sophisticated behaviors associated with in-context learning. Overall, our study provides several insights that indicate large language models may be under-trained for in-context learning and opens up questions on how to pre-train language models to more effectively perform in-context learning.

papers.title: Vocabulary Expansion of Large Language Models via Kullback-Leibler-Based Self-Distillation
papers.research_question: How should new components (embeddings and head) be initialized using a novel student-teacher framework for vocabulary expansion in frozen large language models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a self-distillation method using KL divergence to initialize new token embeddings for vocabulary expansion in frozen LLMs, enabling effective integration of new domain-specific terminology.
papers.conclusion: The proposed vocabulary expansion method via self-distillation is effective and outperforms existing methods, providing a mathematically grounded approach for integrating new tokens into pre-trained LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
The proposed KL-divergence-based self-distillation method outperforms cross-entropy training and heuristic initialization methods on code generation benchmarks.
The method preserves model knowledge and avoids catastrophic forgetting and overfitting.
The cosine similarity analysis shows that KL-optimized embeddings align more with the first composite token, while CE-optimized embeddings align more with the last composite token.
The loss (KL or CE) is a poor proxy for downstream performance, and the initialization strategy significantly impacts results.
The method is robust across different evaluation settings and outperforms the base model and other vocabulary expansion methods.
papers.limitation:
Loss is a poor proxy for LLM performance and functionality, especially during fine-tuning for vocabulary expansion.
The evaluation setup heavily influences outcomes, requiring extensive experimentation to align the evaluation dataset with the model.
future_direction: Training embeddings with a mixture of KL and cross-entropy losses.
Investigating temperature scaling in the softmax layer for student-teacher training.
Further mechanistic interpretation using different metrics and evaluating distinct activations and hidden states.
papers.abstract: Large pre-trained language models often struggle to incorporate new domain-specific terminology when fine-tuned on small, specialized corpora. In this work, we address the challenge of vocabulary expansion in frozen LLMs by introducing a mathematically grounded method for knowledge distillation via KL divergence, even when the original and extended models use different tokenizations. This allows the student model to inherit distributional knowledge from the teacher despite differing vocabularies. We compare our KL-based distillation approach to conventional cross-entropy training, evaluating both methods across multiple strategies for initializing new token embeddings. After embedding initialization, models are further fine-tuned to integrate the new vocabulary. Each trained model is benchmarked on approximately 2000 code-generation tasks, where our approach achieves the best performance across the board. Finally, through mechanistic interpretability, we analyze how models learn representations for the new tokens, providing an explanation for the observed gains and offering insight into the structure of embedding space during vocabulary expansion.

papers.title: What Makes Language Models Good-enough?
papers.research_question: What architectural features, specifically the number of layers and self-attention heads, make language models learn human-like good-enough language processing?
papers.core_contribution: This paper shows that language models with shallower depth and fewer attention heads can exhibit human-like good-enough language processing, indicating that deep architectures are not necessary for such performance.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that shallow transformer architectures can achieve human-like good-enough language processing, while the role of attention heads remains unclear.
papers.key_findings:
Models with shallower depth and fewer attention heads can learn good-enough language processing, similar to full models.
Increasing the number of layers from 8 to 12 does not significantly improve human-like good-enough performance.
The number of attention heads does not clearly contribute to models' good-enough performance, contradicting the hypothesis about working memory.
Human accuracy decreases with increased memory load, and models show a similar pattern, especially for items with correct no answers.
The GELP dataset effectively captures good-enough language processing phenomena in humans and models.
papers.limitation:
Model coverage is limited to BERT.
Use of templates in dataset creation may result in unnatural sentences.
Does not test whether models can perform in a human-like way in terms of both grammatical knowledge and good-enough language processing.
future_direction: Generalizing findings to other Transformer-based models such as GPT-2.
Testing whether models can learn the human-like balance between robust and heuristic language processing.
papers.abstract: Psycholinguistic research suggests that humans may build a representation of linguistic input that is 'good-enough' for the task at hand. This study examines what architectural features make language models learn human-like good-enough language processing. We focus on the number of layers and self-attention heads in Transformers. We create a good-enough language processing (GELP) evaluation dataset (7,680 examples), which is designed to test the effects of two plausibility types, eight construction types, and three degrees of memory cost on language processing. To annotate GELP, we first conduct a crowdsourcing experiment whose design follows prior psycholinguistic studies. Our model evaluation against the annotated GELP then reveals that the full model as well as models with fewer layers and/or self-attention heads exhibit a good-enough performance. This result suggests that models with shallower depth and fewer heads can learn good-enough language processing.

papers.title: The Geometry of Tokens in Internal Representations of Large Language Models
papers.research_question: What is the relationship between the geometry of token embeddings and their role in next token prediction within transformer models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper finds a correlation between the intrinsic dimension of token representations and the cross-entropy loss of next token predictions, indicating that prompts with higher loss have tokens lying in higher-dimensional manifolds.
papers.conclusion: The study connects geometric approaches to interpretability by showing that intrinsic dimension of token representations correlates with cross-entropy loss, suggesting ID as a metric for model performance.
papers.key_findings:
Intrinsic dimension of token representations peaks in early to middle layers, with higher peaks for shuffled data.
Cosine similarity among tokens increases with shuffling, indicating greater alignment of token vectors.
Neighborhood overlap shows that structured data retains more coherent token neighborhoods across layers than shuffled data.
There is a statistical correlation between intrinsic dimension and average cross-entropy loss for next token predictions.
The correlation is explained via a relationship between ID of logits and contextual entropy, and through toy models showing log dimension dependence.
papers.limitation:
Observables computed at low ranges of nearest neighbors; multiscale analysis could reveal more.
Differences in distribution patterns for structured vs shuffled data need further investigation.
future_direction: Multiscale analysis of observables.
Investigation of other geometric observables and their relation to next token probabilities.
Applications to design and training of LLMs for interpretability and efficiency.
papers.abstract: We investigate the relationship between the geometry of token embeddings and their role in the next token prediction within transformer models. An important aspect of this connection uses the notion of empirical measure, which encodes the distribution of token point clouds across transformer layers and drives the evolution of token representations in the mean-field interacting picture. We use metrics such as intrinsic dimension, neighborhood overlap, and cosine similarity to observationally probe these empirical measures across layers. To validate our approach, we compare these metrics to a dataset where the tokens are shuffled, which disrupts the syntactic and semantic structure. Our findings reveal a correlation between the geometric properties of token embeddings and the cross-entropy loss of next token predictions, implying that prompts with higher loss values have tokens represented in higher-dimensional spaces.

papers.title: Scaling Behavior for Large Language Models regarding Numeral Systems: An Example using Pythia
papers.research_question: What is the impact of different numeral systems (base 10, base 100, base 1000) on the scaling behavior and data efficiency of large language models for numeric operations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that a base 10 numeral system is more data-efficient for training LLMs on numeric operations compared to base 100 or base 1000 systems, particularly in from-scratch training.
papers.conclusion: The base 10 numeral system is more data-efficient for LLMs in arithmetic tasks, and this insight can inform tokenization designs.
papers.key_findings:
Base 10 is consistently more data-efficient than base 100 or base 1000 in from-scratch training across data scales and model sizes.
Fine-tuned models perform comparably across numeral systems, with base 10 at least on par.
Extrapolation experiments reveal patterns like truncated addition and base-10 carry extrapolation.
Base 100 and base 1000 systems struggle with token-level discernment and token-level operations in extrapolation.
The superiority of base 10 is more pronounced in multiplication than in addition.
papers.limitation: Scaling behavior analysis requires extensive computational resources, and the study did not perform a thorough hyperparameter grid search, leading to potential instability issues.
papers.abstract: Though Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown remarkable abilities in mathematics reasoning, they are still struggling with performing numeric operations accurately, such as addition and multiplication. Numbers can be tokenized into tokens in various ways by different LLMs and affect the numeric operations performance. Currently, there are two representatives: 1) Tokenize into $1$-digit, and 2) Tokenize into $1\sim 3$ digit. The difference is roughly equivalent to using different numeral systems (namely base $10$ or base $10^{3}$). In light of this, we study the scaling behavior of different numeral systems in the context of transformer-based large language models. We empirically show that a base $10$ system is consistently more data-efficient than a base $10^{2}$ or $10^{3}$ system across training data scale, model sizes under from-scratch training settings, while different number systems have very similar fine-tuning performances. We attribute this to higher token frequencies of a base $10$ system. Additionally, we reveal extrapolation behavior patterns on addition and multiplication. We identify that base $100$ and base $1000$ systems struggle on token-level discernment and token-level operations. We also sheds light on the mechanism learnt by the models.

papers.title: Reasoning Circuits in Language Models: A Mechanistic Interpretation of Syllogistic Inference
papers.research_question: How is content-independent syllogistic reasoning internalized in LMs during pre-training? Are content-independent mechanisms disentangled from world knowledge and belief biases? Does the core reasoning mechanism generalize across syllogistic schemes, model sizes, and architectures?
papers.core_contribution: The paper uncovers a sufficient and necessary circuit for syllogistic reasoning involving middle-term suppression, showing that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms that are susceptible to contamination from world knowledge.
papers.conclusion: LMs learn transferable reasoning mechanisms but such mechanisms are contaminated and suppressed by the world knowledge acquired during pre-training, indicating a lack of generalizable abstract logical primitives.
papers.key_findings:
The circuit for syllogistic reasoning involves a three-stage mechanism: long induction, duplication, suppression, and mover heads.
The circuit is necessary and sufficient for symbolic syllogistic reasoning.
The circuit transfers to non-symbolic arguments but is contaminated by belief biases, with additional attention heads encoding world knowledge.
The circuit generalizes across unconditionally valid syllogistic schemes where models achieve high accuracy.
The suppression mechanism pattern is compatible across different model families and sizes, though with increasing complexity in larger models.
papers.limitation:
The analysis is confined to specific syllogistic reasoning templates and does not consider more complex scenarios.
The experimentation is confined due to the intricate level of granularity and computational complexity required in circuit analysis.
future_direction: Further studies to understand how the discovered symbolic circuit can be effectively disentangled from world knowledge to enable systematic generalization in LMs’ reasoning.
papers.abstract: Recent studies on reasoning in language models (LMs) have sparked a debate on whether they can learn systematic inferential principles or merely exploit superficial patterns in the training data. To understand and uncover the mechanisms adopted for formal reasoning in LMs, this paper presents a mechanistic interpretation of syllogistic inference. Specifically, we present a methodology for circuit discovery aimed at interpreting content-independent and formal reasoning mechanisms. Through two distinct intervention methods, we uncover a sufficient and necessary circuit involving middle-term suppression that elucidates how LMs transfer information to derive valid conclusions from premises. Furthermore, we investigate how belief biases manifest in syllogistic inference, finding evidence of partial contamination from additional attention heads responsible for encoding commonsense and contextualized knowledge. Finally, we explore the generalization of the discovered mechanisms across various syllogistic schemes, model sizes and architectures. The identified circuit is sufficient and necessary for syllogistic schemes on which the models achieve high accuracy (>60%), with compatible activation patterns across models of different families. Overall, our findings suggest that LMs learn transferable content-independent reasoning mechanisms, but that, at the same time, such mechanisms do not involve generalizable and abstract logical primitives, being susceptible to contamination by the same world knowledge acquired during pre-training.

papers.title: Revisiting Prompt Sensitivity in Large Language Models for Text Classification: The Role of Prompt Underspecification
papers.research_question: Is a significant portion of the observed prompt sensitivity in LLMs attributable to prompt underspecification, and how can it be mitigated?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that prompt underspecification is a significant contributor to observed prompt sensitivity in LLMs, and that using well-specified instruction prompts and in-context learning can effectively mitigate this issue.
papers.conclusion: A large part of observed prompt sensitivity is due to the use of underspecified prompts, and this can be effectively addressed by using well-specified instruction prompts and in-context learning, leading to more robust LLM evaluations.
papers.key_findings:
Underspecified prompts exhibit higher performance variance and lower logit values for relevant label tokens compared to instruction prompts.
In-context learning provides the most consistent benefit for mitigating prompt sensitivity and underspecification, especially when combined with instruction-tuned models.
Logit analysis shows that higher label token logit values are a good indicator of prompt quality and correlate with higher accuracy.
Linear probe analysis reveals that internal model representations are only marginally affected by prompt underspecification, with performance issues emerging primarily in the final layers.
Calibration provides similar but less consistent improvements than in-context learning, while the UNK token mitigation strategy often degrades performance.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to three datasets and three model families, which may not generalize to all tasks and models.
Generation evaluation uses simple string matching and regex, which may underestimate model capabilities.
The analysis uses 10 prompt variants per setting, which may not capture the full spectrum of prompt sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are widely used as zero-shot and few-shot classifiers, where task behaviour is largely controlled through prompting. A growing number of works have observed that LLMs are sensitive to prompt variations, with small changes leading to large changes in performance. However, in many cases, the investigation of sensitivity is performed using underspecified prompts that provide minimal task instructions and weakly constrain the model's output space. In this work, we argue that a significant portion of the observed prompt sensitivity can be attributed to prompt underspecification. We systematically study and compare the sensitivity of underspecified prompts and prompts that provide specific instructions. Utilising performance analysis, logit analysis, and linear probing, we find that underspecified prompts exhibit higher performance variance and lower logit values for relevant tokens, while instruction-prompts suffer less from such problems. However, linear probing analysis suggests that the effects of prompt underspecification have only a marginal impact on the internal LLM representations, instead emerging in the final layers. Overall, our findings highlight the need for more rigour when investigating and mitigating prompt sensitivity.

papers.title: The Curious Case of Hallucinatory (Un)answerability: Finding Truths in the Hidden States of Over-Confident Large Language Models
papers.research_question: Do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer?
papers.core_contribution: Large language models encode the answerability of input queries in their hidden states, even when they generate hallucinatory answers, and this information can be extracted via linear probing and beam search relaxation.
papers.conclusion: LLMs internally encode query answerability, and leveraging this information through improved decoding techniques can enhance factual generation and reduce hallucinations.
papers.key_findings:
Prompting with a hint about the possibility of unanswerability substantially improves detection of unanswerable questions (up to 80% F1 gain).
Beam search relaxation reveals that responses acknowledging unanswerability often exist in the beam, even when not the top candidate.
Linear classifiers trained on the last hidden layer's first token representation achieve high F1 (above 75%) in detecting answerability.
The answerability subspace identified by linear classifiers is transferable across different QA datasets.
Erasing the answerability subspace via linear concept erasure modifies model behavior, confirming the subspace's behavioral relevance.
papers.limitation: Performance drops on NQ and MuSiQue due to distribution shift and the increased complexity of multi-hop reasoning.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been shown to possess impressive capabilities, while also raising crucial concerns about the faithfulness of their responses. A primary issue arising in this context is the management of (un)answerable queries by LLMs, which often results in hallucinatory behavior due to overconfidence. In this paper, we explore the behavior of LLMs when presented with (un)answerable queries. We ask: do models represent the fact that the question is (un)answerable when generating a hallucinatory answer? Our results show strong indications that such models encode the answerability of an input query, with the representation of the first decoded token often being a strong indicator. These findings shed new light on the spatial organization within the latent representations of LLMs, unveiling previously unexplored facets of these models. Moreover, they pave the way for the development of improved decoding techniques with better adherence to factual generation, particularly in scenarios where query (un)answerability is a concern.

papers.title: Language Models "Grok" to Copy
papers.research_question: How do language models develop context copying abilities during pre-training, and is this process similar to grokking?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes that language models develop context copying abilities through a process similar to grokking, with evidence from pre-training dynamics.
papers.conclusion: The development of context copying in language models is a form of grokking, offering insights for improving language model training and in-context performance.
papers.key_findings:
Pre-training loss decreases rapidly while context copying ability lags and then abruptly saturates, resembling grokking.
The development of copying ability is independent of the number of tokens trained, similar to grokking speed.
Induction heads form from shallow to deep layers during training, mirroring circuit development in grokking.
Regularization techniques like dropout and weight decay can accelerate or enhance the development of context copying.
papers.limitation: The study focuses on copying tasks and does not evaluate in-context learning (ICL) tasks, which are more complex, due to limited computational resources.
future_direction: Applying the understanding of grokking to improve in-context capacities like ICL in language models.
papers.abstract: We examine the pre-training dynamics of language models, focusing on their ability to copy text from preceding context--a fundamental skill for various LLM applications, including in-context learning (ICL) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). We propose a novel perspective that Transformer-based language models develop copying abilities similarly to grokking, which refers to sudden generalization on test set long after the model fit to the training set. Our experiments yield three arguments: (1) The pre-training loss decreases rapidly, while the context copying ability of models initially lags and then abruptly saturates. (2) The speed of developing copying ability is independent of the number of tokens trained, similarly to how grokking speed is unaffected by dataset size as long as the data distribution is preserved. (3) Induction heads, the attention heads responsible for copying, form from shallow to deep layers during training, mirroring the development of circuits in deeper layers during grokking. We contend that the connection between grokking and context copying can provide valuable insights for more effective language model training, ultimately improving in-context performance. For example, we demonstrated that techniques that enhance grokking, such as regularization, either accelerate or enhance the development of context copying.

papers.title: Generative Models as a Complex Systems Science: How can we make sense of large language model behavior?
papers.research_question: How can we make sense of large language model behavior? The paper argues for a systematic effort to decompose language model behavior into categories that explain cross-task performance, to guide mechanistic explanations.
papers.core_contribution: The paper argues that the field of generative model research should be reconceptualized as a complex systems science, focusing on discovering and categorizing high-level behaviors of models to guide bottom-up mechanistic explanations and future-proof interpretability research.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes by arguing for an increased focus on the foundational question of 'what are models doing?' to guide the classic 'why are models doing that?' question in mechanistic interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Benchmarks alone cannot discover or characterize new model behaviors; they can only measure performance on predefined tasks.
A hierarchical taxonomy of model behavior (e.g., copying, in-context learning) is needed to guide mechanistic interpretability and understand what models are doing in general.
Generative models are easier to study than many naturally arising complex systems because they are simulable, repeatable, and allow for easy perturbation without observer effects.
The field lacks a formal vocabulary for describing model behaviors, which hinders progress in explaining why models work.
papers.limitation: The proposed behavioral approach is conceptual and lacks a concrete, implemented framework for discovering and categorizing behaviors.
future_direction: Developing a rich inventory of behavioral tests to create a universal scaffolding for analyzing any new model.
Investigating possible mappings between training data and generated data to establish new behavioral categories.
Formalizing the concept of 'behavior' and finding metamodels that are both explanatory and simple to describe.
papers.abstract: Coaxing out desired behavior from pretrained models, while avoiding undesirable ones, has redefined NLP and is reshaping how we interact with computers. What was once a scientific engineering discipline-in which building blocks are stacked one on top of the other-is arguably already a complex systems science, in which emergent behaviors are sought out to support previously unimagined use cases. Despite the ever increasing number of benchmarks that measure task performance, we lack explanations of what behaviors language models exhibit that allow them to complete these tasks in the first place. We argue for a systematic effort to decompose language model behavior into categories that explain cross-task performance, to guide mechanistic explanations and help future-proof analytic research.

papers.title: Do Large Language Models Understand Logic or Just Mimick Context?
papers.research_question: Do LLMs understand logical rules to draw inferences, or do they 'guess' the answers by learning a type of probabilistic mapping through context?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs do not truly understand logical rules; in-context learning simply enhances the likelihood of correct answers. Altering context or logical terms significantly disrupts model outputs, indicating reliance on probabilistic associations.
papers.conclusion: While LLMs may improve their logical reasoning performance through in-context learning and methodologies such as COT, these enhancements do not equate to a genuine understanding of logical operations and definitions, nor do they necessarily confer the capability for logical reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Chain of Thought (COT) in-context examples markedly improve the performance of large-scale models on logical reasoning tasks.
Large models demonstrate resilience to distracting elements within in-context examples, while smaller models suffer notable declines in performance when standard in-context examples are not used.
Large models do not genuinely comprehend logical principles; they rely on probabilistic associations between input examples and outputs.
Modifying logical symbols and predicates leads to a low rate of successful adaptation across all model sizes, even with prompt-based or example-based guidance.
Example-based guidance (providing modified examples) improves the modification rate more than prompt-based guidance alone.
papers.limitation: The enhancement in logical reasoning from prompts and in-context examples remains marginal, and current pre-training based on next-token prediction may not be suited for logical tasks.
future_direction: Devising an alternative pre-training strategy tailored to the requirements of logical tasks.
Exploring methods to enhance the model's logical reasoning capabilities independent of context-based examples.
papers.abstract: Over the past few years, the abilities of large language models (LLMs) have received extensive attention, which have performed exceptionally well in complicated scenarios such as logical reasoning and symbolic inference. A significant factor contributing to this progress is the benefit of in-context learning and few-shot prompting. However, the reasons behind the success of such models using contextual reasoning have not been fully explored. Do LLMs have understand logical rules to draw inferences, or do they ``guess'' the answers by learning a type of probabilistic mapping through context? This paper investigates the reasoning capabilities of LLMs on two logical reasoning datasets by using counterfactual methods to replace context text and modify logical concepts. Based on our analysis, it is found that LLMs do not truly understand logical rules; rather, in-context learning has simply enhanced the likelihood of these models arriving at the correct answers. If one alters certain words in the context text or changes the concepts of logical terms, the outputs of LLMs can be significantly disrupted, leading to counter-intuitive responses. This work provides critical insights into the limitations of LLMs, underscoring the need for more robust mechanisms to ensure reliable logical reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: Physics of Language Models: Part 1, Learning Hierarchical Language Structures
papers.research_question: How do language models perform deep reasoning over hierarchical structures, and can we understand their inner workings using synthetic context-free grammars (CFGs)?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that transformers can learn complex context-free grammars and that their hidden states linearly encode non-terminal information, while attention patterns mimic dynamic programming algorithms for parsing.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can learn complex hierarchical structures defined by CFGs, and their internal representations and attention patterns align with dynamic programming algorithms for parsing.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers (GPT variants) can accurately learn and generate strings from synthetic CFGs that require dynamic programming to parse.
Hidden states of the trained transformers linearly encode non-terminal ancestor information almost perfectly.
Attention patterns in the trained models resemble the information flow of dynamic programming, with boundary-based attention.
Relative and rotary positional embeddings are crucial for learning harder CFGs, outperforming absolute positional embeddings.
Training with perturbed data (10% noise) improves robustness to corrupted prefixes.
papers.limitation: The chosen CFGs are synthetic and may not encompass all CFGs; the results are specific to the designed CFG families.
papers.abstract: Transformer-based language models are effective but complex, and understanding their inner workings and reasoning mechanisms is a significant challenge. Previous research has primarily explored how these models handle simple tasks like name copying or selection, and we extend this by investigating how these models perform recursive language structure reasoning defined by context-free grammars (CFGs). We introduce a family of synthetic CFGs that produce hierarchical rules, capable of generating lengthy sentences (e.g., hundreds of tokens) that are locally ambiguous and require dynamic programming to parse. Despite this complexity, we demonstrate that generative models like GPT can accurately learn and reason over CFG-defined hierarchies and generate sentences based on it. We explore the model's internals, revealing that its hidden states precisely capture the structure of CFGs, and its attention patterns resemble the information passing in a dynamic programming algorithm. This paper also presents several corollaries, including showing why absolute positional embeddings is inferior to relative and rotary embeddings; uniform attention alone is surprisingly effective (motivating our follow-up work on Canon layers); encoder-only models (e.g., BERT, DeBERTa) struggle with deep structure reasoning on CFGs compared to autoregressive models (e.g., GPT); and injecting structural or syntactic noise into pretraining data markedly improves robustness to corrupted language prompts.

papers.title: Let's Think Dot by Dot: Hidden Computation in Transformer Language Models
papers.research_question: To what extent can transformers use meaningless filler tokens (e.g., '......') to perform hidden computation and solve algorithmic tasks they cannot solve without intermediate tokens, and under what conditions does this occur?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can use meaningless filler tokens to solve hard algorithmic tasks they fail at without intermediate tokens, showing additional tokens provide computational benefits independent of token meaning, but learning to use filler tokens requires specific, dense supervision.
papers.conclusion: For certain parallelizable problems, transformers achieve improved performance with filler tokens instead of chain-of-thought tokens, meaning intermediate tokens can be used purely for computational capacity rather than faithful serial reasoning.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers achieve perfect accuracy on 3SUM and high accuracy on 2SUM-Transform with filler tokens, while failing without them.
The performance gap between filler and no-filler settings increases with problem complexity (input length and dimension).
Filler token representations encode hidden, task-relevant computation, as shown by fine-tuning experiments.
Learning to use filler tokens is difficult and requires training on parallelizable chain-of-thought data; instance-adaptive CoT data does not transfer.
Filler tokens extend transformer expressive power within the complexity class TC0, enabling solution of problems with deep quantifier nesting.
future_direction: Investigate the extent to which token-parallelizable, TC0 algorithmic problems arise in natural language contexts.

Investigate whether natural-language text provides adequate supervision for filler-token computation, providing parallelizable supervision rather than non-parallelizable, instance-adaptive chains of thought.
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought responses from language models improve performance across most benchmarks. However, it remains unclear to what extent these performance gains can be attributed to human-like task decomposition or simply the greater computation that additional tokens allow. We show that transformers can use meaningless filler tokens (e.g., '......') in place of a chain of thought to solve two hard algorithmic tasks they could not solve when responding without intermediate tokens. However, we find empirically that learning to use filler tokens is difficult and requires specific, dense supervision to converge. We also provide a theoretical characterization of the class of problems where filler tokens are useful in terms of the quantifier depth of a first-order formula. For problems satisfying this characterization, chain-of-thought tokens need not provide information about the intermediate computational steps involved in multi-token computations. In summary, our results show that additional tokens can provide computational benefits independent of token choice. The fact that intermediate tokens can act as filler tokens raises concerns about large language models engaging in unauditable, hidden computations that are increasingly detached from the observed chain-of-thought tokens.

papers.title: Understanding In-Context Learning from Repetitions
papers.research_question: What is the mechanism underpinning in-context learning in Large Language Models, and how can it be understood through the lens of surface repetitions and token co-occurrence reinforcement?
papers.core_contribution: This paper provides a novel feature-centric perspective on in-context learning by identifying and analyzing token co-occurrence reinforcement, showing how surface patterns both enable and hinder ICL.
papers.conclusion: Token reinforcement is a key mechanism in in-context learning, acting as a double-edged sword that can be leveraged to maximize ICL effectiveness with informed demonstrations.
papers.key_findings:
Token co-occurrence reinforcement exists: the connection between any two tokens strengthens with their contextual co-occurrences.
Token reinforcement helps constrain the output space and enables models to follow patterns like chain-of-thought prompting.
Token reinforcement can lead to spurious connections and cause ICL failures when demonstrations contain unintended patterns.
The reinforcement effect scales with model size, with larger models showing stronger distant reinforcement.
Token reinforcement arises from the model's optimization of training likelihood, as evidenced by empirical analysis of pretraining data.
papers.abstract: This paper explores the elusive mechanism underpinning in-context learning in Large Language Models (LLMs). Our work provides a novel perspective by examining in-context learning via the lens of surface repetitions. We quantitatively investigate the role of surface features in text generation, and empirically establish the existence of \emph{token co-occurrence reinforcement}, a principle that strengthens the relationship between two tokens based on their contextual co-occurrences. By investigating the dual impacts of these features, our research illuminates the internal workings of in-context learning and expounds on the reasons for its failures. This paper provides an essential contribution to the understanding of in-context learning and its potential limitations, providing a fresh perspective on this exciting capability.

papers.title: Large Language Models as Neurolinguistic Subjects: Discrepancy between Performance and Competence
